title: What makes an object eligible for garbage collection — no live (strong) reference chain from any GC root — and what are the common ways to make an object eligible (nulling the reference, reassigning it, letting the variable go out of scope, and island of isolation where a group of objects reference only each other but no external root reaches them)?
shortTitle: What makes an object eligible for garbage collection?

s1_definition.profdef: An object becomes eligible for garbage collection when it is no longer reachable through any chain of strong references starting from a garbage collection root, such as a live thread's stack frame, a static field, or a JNI reference. The garbage collector uses reachability, not reference counting, as its criterion. Common ways to make an object eligible are setting its only reference to null, reassigning that reference to another object, letting the referencing local variable go out of scope, and the island-of-isolation case, where a cluster of objects still reference each other but no external GC root can reach the cluster, so the entire island is collectable despite the internal references.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of GC roots as the senior managers who are physically present in the bank, and every active account file is only kept if a manager can trace a path of hands to it, one person holding a folder that references another folder, and so on. The moment no manager can trace any path of hands to a file, that file is shredded, because nobody alive is using it. The island of isolation is a stack of folders in a locked back room that all cite each other in their footnotes, but no manager outside the room holds any thread leading in. Even though the folders reference each other, the whole stack is shredded together, because mutual reference among unreachable things does not keep them alive.
s1_definition.oneliner: An object is collectable when no strong reference chain from a GC root reaches it, and even objects that reference each other form a collectable island if nothing outside reaches them.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** An object becomes eligible for garbage collection when it is no longer reachable through any chain of strong references starting from a garbage collection root, such as a live thread's stack frame, a static field, or a JNI reference. The garbage collector uses reachability, not reference counting, as its criterion. Common ways to make an object eligible are setting its only reference to null, reassigning that reference to another object, letting the referencing local variable go out of scope, and the island-of-isolation case, where a cluster of objects still reference each other but no external GC root can reach the cluster, so the entire island is collectable despite the internal references.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of GC roots as the senior managers who are physically present in the bank, and every active account file is only kept if a manager can trace a path of hands to it, one person holding a folder that references another folder, and so on. The moment no manager can trace any path of hands to a file, that file is shredded, because nobody alive is using it. The island of isolation is a stack of folders in a locked back room that all cite each other in their footnotes, but no manager outside the room holds any thread leading in. Even though the folders reference each other, the whole stack is shredded together, because mutual reference among unreachable things does not keep them alive.

**One line to remember:** An object is collectable when no strong reference chain from a GC root reaches it, and even objects that reference each other form a collectable island if nothing outside reaches them.

sections.s2_technical:
The Java garbage collector decides what to keep using reachability analysis. It starts from a set of GC roots, which include local variables and parameters on the stacks of live threads, static fields of loaded classes, active JNI references, and a few internal structures. From these roots it traverses every strong reference and marks everything it can reach as live. Anything not marked is unreachable and therefore eligible for collection. This is why Java does not suffer from the classic reference-counting leak where two objects pointing at each other keep each other alive forever.

The simplest way to make an object eligible is to null out its only reference. For example, `Account a = new Account(...); a = null;` leaves the Account with no reference from the stack, so if nothing else refers to it, it becomes eligible immediately. Reassignment works the same way: `a = new Account(...)` points `a` at a new object, and the previous object it referenced becomes eligible if no other reference survives.

Letting a variable go out of scope is the most common and natural cause. When a method returns, its local variables vanish from the stack, so any object referenced only by those locals loses its last root path and becomes eligible. For instance, a temporary `Account` created inside a `transfer` method and never stored anywhere is eligible the moment the method returns. This is the everyday mechanism by which most short-lived objects are reclaimed.

The island of isolation is the interesting case that proves reachability beats reference counting. Suppose object A references B and B references A, and perhaps a third object C is tangled in too, all pointing at each other. If the single external reference that reached this cluster is then removed, the cluster still has internal references, so a naive reference-counting scheme would think each object is still in use and never free them. Java's reachability collector instead asks a different question: can any GC root reach this cluster? If the answer is no, the entire island is unreachable and all of it is collected together, mutual references notwithstanding. A concrete example is two linked `Account` nodes in a doubly linked ledger list that reference each other as previous and next; once the list head reference is dropped and no root reaches the pair, both nodes are collected despite still pointing at each other.

Several senior-level nuances matter. Eligibility does not mean immediate collection; the object is reclaimed only when the collector next runs, and you cannot force this, since `System.gc()` is merely a hint. There are reference strengths beyond strong, namely soft, weak, and phantom, which deliberately do not prevent collection and are used for caches and cleanup. A very common real leak is an object that stays reachable by accident, for example a listener still held in a static list or an entry never removed from a long-lived map, which keeps it alive even though you are "done" with it. The practical discipline is to let scope do the work, avoid holding references longer than needed, and be careful with static collections and caches that can silently pin objects as reachable forever.
sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India our customers are Rajesh, a software engineer with savings account SAV2001 holding ten lakh rupees, and Priya, a property owner with current account CUR3001 holding two lakh fifty thousand rupees.

Problem 1 — during end-of-day processing we create many temporary statement objects, and memory was climbing because a developer kept every temporary statement in a static list "just in case." Those objects stayed reachable from a static GC root forever, so they were never collected. We want to show how letting references go out of scope, nulling them, and not pinning them in a static collection makes them eligible for collection.

Problem 2 — our ledger uses a small doubly linked structure where each transaction node points to the previous and next node. When we discard an old day's ledger, the nodes still reference each other, and we want to prove that this mutual referencing does not keep them alive. As long as no external root reaches the chain, the whole island is collectable. We want to demonstrate this island of isolation explicitly.

Our runnable demo will define an `Account` with debit and credit, a `LedgerNode` that references a previous and next node to form an island, and a `GcDemo` main that performs a transfer from Rajesh to Priya, then shows three eligibility paths: nulling a reference, letting a scoped temporary go out of scope by returning from a helper, and building a two-node linked island whose head reference is then dropped. We will use `WeakReference` as a detector to log when each object is actually reclaimed after a GC hint.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh (SAV2001, 1000000), Priya (CUR3001, 250000), a rent amount of 50000, plus temporary objects used to demonstrate each eligibility path.

Step 1 — the transfer runs. Rajesh is debited 50000 to 950000 and Priya is credited 50000 to 300000. These two accounts stay reachable from `main`'s stack, so they are not eligible for collection yet.

Step 2 — path one creates a temporary account and watches it with a weak reference. Setting the only strong reference to null removes its last root path, so it becomes eligible. After a GC hint the weak reference reports it was collected.

Step 3 — path two calls a helper that creates a scoped account and returns only a weak reference to it. When the helper returns, the local variable holding the strong reference disappears from the stack, so the account goes out of scope and becomes eligible. After a GC hint it is reported collected.

Step 4 — path three builds two ledger nodes and links them so each references the other, forming an island. Weak references watch both. Setting both external variables to null means no GC root reaches either node, even though they still reference each other. After a GC hint both nodes are reported collected, proving mutual references do not save an unreachable island.

Final output:

```text
2026-10-30 19:29:03 INFO    Transfer 50000 SUCCESS, Rajesh=950000 Priya=300000
2026-10-30 19:29:03 INFO    PATH 1 (nulled reference) → collected? true
2026-10-30 19:29:03 INFO    PATH 2 (out of scope) → collected? true
2026-10-30 19:29:03 INFO    PATH 3 head (island) → collected? true
2026-10-30 19:29:03 INFO    PATH 3 tail (island) → collected? true
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
An object becomes eligible for garbage collection when it is no longer reachable through any chain of strong references starting from a garbage collection root. The roots are things like the local variables on the stacks of live threads, static fields of loaded classes, and active native references. The collector starts at those roots, follows every strong reference, and marks everything it can reach as live; anything it cannot reach is eligible for collection. The key insight is that Java uses reachability, not reference counting, which is why it does not suffer from the classic cycle leak.

There are a few everyday ways an object becomes eligible. You can null out its only reference, you can reassign that reference to point at something else, or, most commonly, you can simply let the referencing local variable go out of scope when a method returns. A temporary object created inside a method and never stored anywhere becomes eligible the instant the method returns, and this is how the vast majority of short-lived objects get reclaimed without any effort on my part.

The island of isolation is the case that proves reachability beats reference counting. If a group of objects all reference each other but the single external reference that reached the group is removed, a naive reference-counting collector would see the internal references and keep them alive forever. Java instead asks whether any GC root can reach the group, and if the answer is no, the entire island is collected together despite the mutual references. A doubly linked ledger where each node points to the previous and next node is a perfect example; once the head reference is dropped and no root reaches the chain, the whole chain is freed.

A couple of nuances I always mention are that eligibility is not the same as immediate collection, because the object is only reclaimed when the collector next runs and System.gc is just a hint, and that the most common real leak is an object staying reachable by accident, typically because it is still held in a static collection or a long-lived map.

At National Bank of India this was not theoretical. During end-of-day processing our memory kept climbing because a developer stashed every temporary statement object in a static list "just in case," which kept them reachable from a static root forever, so they were never collected. The fix was to stop pinning them and let scope do its job, after which they became eligible and were reclaimed normally. Separately, when we discard an old day's ledger built as a doubly linked chain of nodes that reference each other, I was able to reassure the team that the mutual references do not matter: as long as no external root reaches the chain, the whole island is collected together, and we verified exactly that with weak references in a small demo.

---

keyPoints: No live reference chain from any GC root to the object
Setting reference to null: obj = null — IF no other reference exists
Island of isolation: group of objects referencing only each other, no external reference
Reassignment: obj = new Other() — old object eligible if no other refs
Exiting a method: local references go out of scope — their objects may become eligible
